title: Body Language And Classroom Management https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2009/09/07/body-language-and-classroom-management/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that while rules, consequences, and follow-through form the foundation of classroom management, true effectiveness comes from building 'leverage,' or influence, and that body language is a significant, often overlooked source of that leverage. Citing the widely used statistic that speech accounts for only a small fraction of communicated meaning, he offers a short guide to five specific body language elements: eye contact, facial expressions, posture, proximity, and touch. For each, he explains both the benefit of using it well (trust, confidence, persuasion) and the risk of misuse (intimidation from too much eye contact, aggression from invading personal space). He closes by encouraging teachers to reflect on what their current body language communicates and to experiment deliberately with the recommendations to build more influence with students.
points: Leverage, or influence, is what separates merely adequate classroom management from truly effective classroom management.
Eye contact builds trust and rapport but can intimidate, especially shy students, if overused.
Confident, upright posture signals leadership and makes instructions more likely to be believed and followed.
Standing too close to a student ('proximity') reads as dominance and tends to reduce long-term leverage even if it works momentarily.
A brief, appropriate touch can build rapport and persuasive power when used naturally in conversation.
quotes: Leverage simply means having great influence with your students. This is where the real power comes from. It explains how a teacher can take over a classroom of students from a tough neighborhood, given up on and deemed uncontrollable, and turn them into a dream class.
Seven percent. That’s how much speaking impacts your students. The other 93 percent is attributed to non-verbal communication.

Longer eye contact is associated with trust, good feelings, and rapport—all of which are important leveraging qualities. Be aware, however, that too much eye contact can be intimidating, especially for shy students.
But moving into someone’s personal space without permission is a show of dominance. It’s aggressive and antagonistic and is universally perceived as a threat.
The difference between telling a student to go to time-out with a tall comportment versus saying it with a sagging, defeated posture is night and day.
I’m certain you will look and feel more attractive and confident, resulting in greater leverage with your students and more effective classroom management.
